Flight time check
Test by Faris Sadik · public pages only · not affiliated with the operator

Live test, 17 November 2026. Flight Network app in ChatGPT, checked against se.flightnetwork.com.

Same flight, same fare, one hour apart.

I ran 25 flight searches in your Flight Network app inside ChatGPT and opened the link each answer gives to your own website. In 6 the chat shows a different hour than the website. In 6 more the digits match, but the chat presents them as UTC.

Shown first to the people who own the product, on 17 November 2026.

+1 hand the next date
ChatGPT tells the traveller, SK 171, 586 SEK23:15 → 00:15, 16 Dec
Your website, same flight, same fare22:15 → 23:15, 15 Dec

In the cases I saw, the chat time is later than the real one. A traveller who plans from the chat alone would be an hour late for the real departure. The booking page still shows the right time.

What the 25 searches showed

Each code is one search; select it to see both screens. 7 of the 20 searches I planned in advance had one of the two faults. The other 5 I picked afterwards to test the explanation below.

The same search, ten more times

One run per route says where the fault is, not how often. So I repeated Stockholm to Gothenburg ten times, a new chat each time.

8 of 10 showed 23:15 for the 22:15 flight. 1 was right. 1 ended in a ChatGPT error with no answer.

The right answer is the slow one

From sending the question to a finished answer took a median of 43 seconds across the 9 answers. The eight wrong ones took 39 to 45. The one right answer took 88 seconds, because the model went to the web to check the schedule before it trusted the tool.

Timed in the browser, so it includes the app's permission prompt. Ten runs on one route; it is a first measurement, not a benchmark.

Why it happens

The tool hands the model a local time with a UTC label. ChatGPT quoted the field in 10 conversations, 17 flights. All carry the Z, and all match the local time on your website.

search_flightsZurich to Rome, 15 DecemberLabel wrong
Z means UTC. Your website shows this flight leaving Zurich at 07:10 local time.

Result, as quoted by ChatGPT

{ "dep": { "iata": "ZRH", "time": "2026-12-15T07:10:00Z" }, "arr": { "iata": "FCO", "time": "2026-12-15T08:40:00Z" }, "durationMinutes": 90 }

Why only some answers go wrong

The model checks the times against the flight's duration. That only exposes the label when the two airports are in different time zones.

Different time zones 1 of 11 faulty

London to Stockholm: read as UTC, a 2 h 25 flight would take 3 h 25. The model sees the clash and trusts the duration.

Same time zone 11 of 12 faulty

Stockholm to Gothenburg: one hour either way. Nothing clashes, so the model believes the label. Five answers moved the clock and six kept the digits and called them UTC. The one right answer, Tokyo to Seoul, came after the model looked the schedule up on the web.

Send the same digits with the airport's own offset. Accept or reject the change to see what ChatGPT showed the traveller with each format.

Winner: B, the offset. Right local times in every trial, with no caveat from the model.

The line this touches

The image published with the Flight MCP press release shows a flight card with the line "Times shown in local time". That is the right promise. In 6 of 25 searches the chat says local time and shows a different hour than your website, so the product does not yet keep it every time.

A stopgap until the field is fixed: one sentence in the tool description saying the times are local. I tried it three times with the Z left in. The digits came out right all three times, and all three answers told the traveller that the Z conflicts with the description. It buys time; it does not remove the fault, and it would not help a client that parses the field with a date library.

What I am not claiming

  • Nobody was booked on a wrong flight. The link from the chat lands on your website, where the times are right.
  • I have not seen the tool's response myself, only ChatGPT's quote of it. MCP access is by application.
  • This is 25 searches on one day and ten repeats of one route. It shows the fault exists, where, and that it repeats; it does not show how often your travellers meet it across your traffic.

Check it yourself in two minutes

  1. Open ChatGPT with the Flight Network app added.
  2. Ask for one-way flights from Stockholm Arlanda to Gothenburg on 15 December 2026.
  3. Open the Flight Network link in the answer and compare the departure times.

The answer varies from run to run. Routes inside one time zone are where it fails.

One field, two rules, one test.

The model is being asked to guess what a timestamp means. The fix is to stop making it guess, at the one place that writes the field.

The rule

  1. Departure and arrival are the airport's local clock time and carry that airport's UTC offset.
  2. Arrival minus departure equals the duration field.

Rule 1 makes the label true. Rule 2 catches a wrong time zone table, a wrong date at midnight and a daylight saving slip before a traveller does.

The change

# today (quoted by ChatGPT, search 27) "dep":{"iata":"ZRH","time":"2026-12-15T07:10:00Z"} "arr":{"iata":"FCO","time":"2026-12-15T08:40:00Z"} "durationMinutes":90 # proposed "dep":{"iata":"ZRH","time":"2026-12-15T07:10:00+01:00"} "arr":{"iata":"FCO","time":"2026-12-15T08:40:00+01:00"} "durationMinutes":90

What the tool returned, as quoted

17 flights from 10 searches, quoted by ChatGPT from the tool. Every one breaks rule 1. Every one has the digits your website shows as local time.

Run the two rules on every website row

A wider but weaker check: for each of the 25 searches the page takes every flight on the website's first page (211 rows), writes it in the quoted shape and again with the offset, and applies the two rules. Because the rows are rebuilt and not quoted, this shows the rule and the fix behave as intended across time zones. It is not further proof of what the tool returns. The same check is in the Python package with 9 tests.

Not run yet.

The nineteen A/B trials

Same prompt, the same three flights per route, a new chat each time. ChatGPT, GPT-6.1 Sol, Medium, 17 November 2026. The first flight is 07:10 to 08:40 from Zurich and 06:40 to 10:05 from London.

One thing the table shows that the headline hides: London to Stockholm with Z went three different ways. In the live search the model corrected it. Pasted, it kept the right digits under a UTC heading twice and moved the arrival an hour once. The same payload gets a different answer from run to run. With the offset there was one answer, the right one, all eight times.

With Z: A1 to A5, C1 to C3, then the stopgap E1 to E3

With the offset: B1 to B5, D1 to D3

Why not fix it in the prompt

A sentence in the tool description such as "times are local" would help ChatGPT today. It would not help the next client that parses the field with a date library, and that client will be right to read Z as UTC. The field is the contract. The model's own repair works in 10 of 11 cross-zone searches and in 1 of 12 same-zone ones, which is a measurement of how far a prompt can carry a wrong field.

The prototype: checks in code before the model may show an offer.

Flightcheck is the check I built before the live test: a Python MCP server with three tools where time, duration and price are computed and checked in code before any model may draw an offer. Rule 2 on the previous tab is its duration check. Start on Try it, change the landing time and watch the flight be held.

What it catches

A record whose times and duration disagree, as on London to Stockholm. A price that does not add up. Baggage that is not stated: payment stays closed until the traveller has read it.

What it would have missed

Stockholm to Gothenburg. When both airports share a zone, a local time labelled UTC still adds up, so this check passes it. That is what the live test taught me, and why rule 1 on the previous tab exists.

Its records are example data with invented airlines, and one record uses the values on the image published with the Flight MCP press release. The live finding on this page does not depend on it.

Drawn from the outside: the public AI Solutions page names the MCP endpoint, and the website shows the same flights with local times. The boxes inside your systems are my assumption.

Spec, five lines

  1. Change. The response serialiser writes local time with the airport's offset. No other field changes.
  2. Contract test. The two rules run in CI on every response fixture. Package included: contract.py, 9 tests.
  3. Canary, tier 1. Daily, the two rules on the MCP response for the 25 routes. No model involved.
  4. Canary, tier 2. Weekly, the same 25 routes through the app in ChatGPT, each answer compared with the website. This is what I did by hand.
  5. Acceptance. Tier 1 passes 25 of 25 on three consecutive days. Tier 2 matches the website on 25 of 25 and no answer mentions a UTC marker.

What I need from business owners

  • Which surface is the ground truth when the website and the API disagree. I used the website.
  • Which markets and routes matter most, so the canary set reflects sales and not my guesses.
  • Whether a wrong time in the chat has reached customer service yet, and under which contact reason.
  • Who owns the wording of the tool description that the model reads.

What this test can and cannot carry.

Also seen, not verified: fares

In 14 of 100 matched flights the fare in the chat differs from the fare on the website row, by 2 to 31 SEK, in searches 2, 11, 12, 17 and 27.

I match flights by time and duration, not flight number, and the two pages load a minute apart, so some of this may be my matching or a price that moved. I report it as an observation and would check it with your data before calling it a fault.

How it was run

  • One ChatGPT account, model GPT-6.1 Sol at Medium, Swedish market, 17 November 2026.
  • One prompt for every search: one-way, 15 December 2026, one adult, economy, nonstop flights with flight number, times, duration and fare.
  • Each answer's own Flight Network link was opened and the times read off the result page.
  • A script matches each flight ChatGPT listed to a website row with the same duration and classifies the search. I set one thing by hand: whether the answer presents its times as local or as UTC. The quoted note is shown for each search.
  • 27 searches were run. Two returned no nonstop flights and are shown as void.

What weakens it

  • Searches 1 to 22 were planned in advance: 7 of 20 wrong. Searches 23 to 27 were chosen after I had seen the first 22, to test the same-zone explanation: 5 of 5 wrong. They replaced three planned routes I dropped. The 12 of 25 total includes them.
  • The answer changes between runs. A repeat will not give the same split, and a newer model may repair more or fewer.
  • The tool's response was never seen directly, only as quoted by ChatGPT in 10 searches. A model can misquote; the quotes agree with the website in all 17 cases.
  • 8 of 108 listed flights were not on the first page of website results, so those rows are unchecked.
  • The wide rule check uses rows rebuilt from the website, so its 23 of 25 follows from the time zones and proves nothing new about the tool.
  • The summer search is one search. The fare differences are unverified.
  • No second day. Everything here is 17 November 2026. The ten repeats are one route only.
  • The A/B pasted the payload as text. It was not delivered through the app, and it covers two routes.
  • In every capture where it is visible, the app's own result card shows an error and did not load. I could not rule out my browser, so I do not count it as a finding.
  • All travel dates are in winter. Summer time adds a second way for a fixed offset to be wrong, which is what rule 2 is for.
